The must-sees

  • Arc de Triomphe

    Building · 1836

    Commissioned in 1806 after Austerlitz, it was finished in 1836. The Unknown Soldier was buried under the vault in 1921, and the flame has burned there since 1923.

    Look for: On the side facing the Champs-Élysées, find François Rude’s relief of the volunteers of 1792, known as La Marseillaise.

  • Eiffel Tower

    Building · 1889

    Gustave Eiffel’s company raised it in two years. Many artists called it a smokestack; it stayed, and it is still the tallest structure in the city center.

    Look for: Below the first-floor balcony, the names of 72 French scientists and engineers are written in gold letters around all four sides.

  • Les Invalides

    Museum

    Louis XIV founded it in 1670 as a home for old and wounded soldiers, and many of its buildings still serve veterans. Napoleon’s remains were brought back from Saint Helena in 1840 and lie beneath the dome.

    Look for: Under the dome, Napoleon’s red stone sarcophagus sits in an open circular crypt, so everyone looks down on it from the balustrade.

  • Louvre

    Museum · 1793

    The Louvre was a fortress, then the king’s residence, before the court moved to Versailles. The glass pyramid arrived in 1989 as the new front door.

    Look for: Below ground, you can walk along the moat and stone foundations of the medieval fortress built by Philippe Auguste.

  • Musée d’Orsay

    Museum · 1986

    The Gare d’Orsay opened for the 1900 exposition and closed as a station in 1939. It became a museum of art from 1848 to 1914.

    Look for: On the upper floor, stand behind one of the great station clocks and look out through its glass face over the Seine to Montmartre.

  • Notre-Dame

    Church · 1345

    Begun in 1163, Notre-Dame set the pattern for French Gothic. The 2019 fire destroyed the spire and roof; the rebuilt cathedral reopened in 2024.

    Look for: On the square in front, find Point Zéro, a bronze star in the paving from which road distances across France are measured.

  • Opéra Garnier

    Culture · 1875

    Opened in 1875, it was the social stage of the Third Republic as much as a theater. A lake under the building fed the Phantom legend.

    Look for: High on the roof above the stage, a gilded Apollo holds his lyre up to the sky.

  • Place des Vosges

    Square · 1612

    Henri IV laid it out in 1605 as the Place Royale. Victor Hugo lived at number 6; the arcades still make a complete circuit.

    Look for: Find the two taller pavilions facing each other across the square: the King’s on the south side, the Queen’s on the north.

  • Sacré-Cœur

    Church · 1914

    Built after the Franco-Prussian War as a national vow, it was finished in 1914. The terrace in front looks over the whole city.

    Look for: Inside, look up at the apse mosaic of Christ with his arms spread wide, one of the largest mosaics in France.

  • Sainte-Chapelle

    Church · 1248

    Louis IX raised it in the 1240s inside the royal palace. The upper chapel is almost entirely window, a lantern of biblical scenes.

    Look for: The lower chapel, for palace staff, has a low vaulted ceiling painted blue and scattered with gold fleurs-de-lis.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Paris and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Paris passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
